title: The heart and the reason
about: Pascal died in 1662 and left notes, many of them for a defense of Christianity; they were printed eight years later as his *Pensées*, or thoughts. W. F. Trotter’s English, printed here, follows an edition that numbers over nine hundred notes and sorts them by subject into fourteen sections; that order is an editor’s, not Pascal’s. Pascal writes in his own voice, at times to an unbeliever addressed as *you*. The third passage answers a speaker who has just said the right thing is not to bet at all.

view.says: In 1939 Auden called Pascal by far the noblest and most tempting of the dualists, who in his account split what exists in two, good and evil; Pascal’s kind sets a supernatural world against this one. Auden saw a divided man, corrupt in heart and sound in intellect, and held that his reason saved him, not the heart he credited: reason told him how corrupt his heart was.
view.quote: Like most of us he exalted the faculty he lacked over the faculty he possessed, the heart over the reason
view.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 31 and 46–48
view.checked: Read by the poet in the Internet Archive’s search-inside snippets of the scan prolificdevourer00aude (OCR), pieced together from overlapping snippets, and read again the same way by the examiner on 2026-10-03, forward and backward from each sentence. The page numbers come from the foot lines that fall inside the snippets (the book’s title and the number on odd pages, the number and the author’s name on even ones): the line for p. 45 breaks the sentence on Pascal and Rousseau after its first clause; the line for p. 46 stands in the two Gods passage just before its closing words about the prudent man; and the line for p. 47 falls inside the last clause of the sentence on what saved Pascal, so the sentences on the dualists, the two faculties and the divided man are on p. 47 and the last clause runs on to p. 48; the passage on two worlds and two Gods is on p. 46, with its last sentence and a half on p. 47. That the number line stands at the foot of the page, and that p. 47 ends at those words, is also the finding of remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, section 1.1. remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 11 and appendix H13, gives pp. 46-47 for the dualists sentences. What a dualist is: Auden’s own account of the false philosophy, which starts from a division of the whole in two, one part good with a right to exist and the other evil with none, and may be theological, metaphysical or political; it stands between the foot lines for pp. 30 and 31, so on p. 31 (examiner, 2026-10-03). Pascal’s kind: the two-worlds passage of pp. 46-47; p. 34 (between the foot lines for 33 and 34, the second misread by the OCR) calls him an ascetic dualist, and p. 73 speaks of the old dualism of the natural and supernatural worlds. ‘By far the noblest and most tempting’ paraphrases his two superlatives, the second of which is the word seductive. The split being of p. 47 is, in his sentence, the neurotic child Pascal had been. The quotation’s punctuation was not seen on a printed page.

lenses.label: Reasons
lenses.name: antanaclasis
lenses.plain: the same word said again with a different meaning
lenses.caption: The first sentence uses one word twice, reasons and then reason, in two senses. The plural means grounds or motives; the singular names the power by which a person knows and judges, and it returns three times below. Littré’s French dictionary lists the two senses apart and quotes this sentence under motive. The play on the word is Pascal’s: raisons, raison. It gives the heart reasons in the very word that names the power said not to know them. In the manuscript the clause about reason is an addition above the line, and the play came with it. Auden’s judgment was that Pascal set the heart above the reason.
lenses.why: One word in two senses credits the heart with reasons and says that reason, the knowing power, does not know them; the clause is an addition in the manuscript, and Auden says Pascal set the heart above the reason.

lenses.caption: Trotter, the translator, writes feel, experiences and felt. Behind feel is sait, knows. Behind experiences is sent, from sentir, a verb that means to feel and also to perceive. Behind felt is sensible, able to be perceived, and Littré’s dictionary quotes this phrase under that sense. In fragment 282 Pascal uses sentir for the heart’s knowledge of first principles, where Trotter writes intuitive knowledge, and says that truth is known by the heart as well as by the reason. So the heart here knows as well as loves. Auden’s sentence on Pascal calls both heart and reason faculties.
lenses.why: Behind Trotter’s verbs of feeling are Pascal’s words for knowing and perceiving, one of them his verb for the heart’s knowledge of first principles: the heart knows, as fragment 282 says, and Auden calls both heart and reason faculties.

lenses.label: Against
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: The second fragment, 278, says one thing twice, each time by a contrast: the heart, and not the reason. The second statement is a definition, This, then, is faith, and like the first it ends on the reason that is shut out. Between the two, heart and God change places. In the French edition used here the fragment is one sentence, and then is Trotter’s word. The next fragment says what is denied: faith is God’s gift and not a gift of reasoning. Auden’s verdict uses the same two nouns the other way round: Pascal believed his heart had saved him, and Auden gives the credit to his reason.
lenses.why: The fragment says by a double contrast that faith is the heart’s and not the reason’s, ending each time on the reason it shuts out; Auden’s judgment of Pascal sets the same two words against each other and reverses them.

grounds.claim: heart, God and the closing phrase that denies reason, in each of the two statements

lenses.caption: Both fragments stand on one of the four manuscript pages of the wager, 278 in the margin, 277 upside down at the top. The main text there is late in the dialogue: an unbeliever says he cannot believe, and is told that reason brings him to belief and that he should work on his passions. Modern editors count the two as separate notes, not part of the dialogue, and judge that 278 came first and that Pascal turned the sheet, for want of room, to write 277. The arrangement printed here is an earlier editor’s: it sorts the page’s eight pieces into five of fourteen sections and sets 277 before 278.
lenses.why: The two fragments are separate notes on a page of the wager, beside the exchange in which reason brings the unbeliever to belief and he cannot believe; their order and section are an editor’s; modern editors think 278 the earlier.

lenses.label: Reed
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.caption: Man is called a reed, and the next six words say why: nothing in nature is weaker. Calling one thing by another’s name is metaphor. After the semicolon the reed returns with one word added, thinking, so one image holds both things the paragraph argues: first the weakness, then the thought. The editor of the French text finds a memory of Montaigne in the vapour and the drop of water, and quotes him on man overthrown by a contrary wind or a morning mist. A note of Pascal’s headed Montaigne begins by calling his faults great. Auden wrote that Pascal was to him what Montaigne had been to Pascal.
lenses.why: One image holds weakness and thought together, and the paragraph argues them in turn; the editor traces the weakness to Montaigne, whose faults Pascal calls great, and Auden says he felt about Pascal as Pascal felt about Montaigne.

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: The verbs of force belong to the universe, or to a vapour and a drop of water: arm, crush, kill, killed. Four times their object is him. Man’s own verbs are few: he is, he dies, he knows. The last clause gives the universe the same verb with nothing after it, and that verb is the whole reason given for more noble, which the editor of the French text glosses as of a higher kind. The next paragraph concludes with then: all dignity is in thought. That is Pascal’s word; Auden’s word for the faculty Pascal possessed is reason, and he held that it, not the heart, saved him.
lenses.why: The universe has the verbs of force and man the verb to know, which is the reason given for calling him more noble; the conclusion puts all dignity in thought, and Auden held that Pascal’s reason saved him.

lenses.label: Crossing
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order
lenses.caption: The last sentence has two halves, each opening with by. In the first the universe acts on me; in the second I act on the world. The two come back in crossed order, which is chiasmus. In Pascal’s French one verb serves both halves, comprend and comprends. It means to contain and to understand, and the French editor notes that Pascal sets the literal sense against the figurative: what holds the speaker in space, he holds in thought. The heart’s reasons turn on one word in the same way. Trotter needs two verbs, encompasses and comprehend. In the manuscript By space is an addition, which gave the halves matching openings.
lenses.why: The two halves name universe and speaker in crossed order, and in French one verb, to contain and to understand, serves both: what holds him in space he holds in thought. Pascal added the opening words.

grounds.claim: the universe and the speaker, named in one order and then the other; the two verbs; the two openings with by

lenses.label: Voice
lenses.caption: The passage is one side of a conversation: the other speaker has refused to bet. Three statements rule that out: you must wager, not optional, You are embarked. Then come two questions, four invitations with let us, and one point called settled, in a sentence Pascal added above the line. You or your comes eighteen times in Trotter’s English and fifteen in the French, I not once, so the choosing stays with the listener. One of Pascal’s notes is headed Order by dialogues. Auden granted such accounts of choice their interest as drama and asked if they are true: his decisive choices hardly seemed serious when he made them.
lenses.why: The argument is speech to a you who has objected, so the choice stays with the listener; Pascal has a note headed Order by dialogues, and Auden granted such accounts their interest as drama and asked if they are true.

lenses.label: Pairs
lenses.name: parallelism
lenses.plain: clauses of the same build, set side by side
lenses.caption: Three clauses are built alike, which is parallelism: two things to lose, two things to stake, two things to shun. They head four pairs, each divided the same way. One side reads the true, reason, knowledge, error. The other reads the good, will, happiness, misery. The division lets the argument settle reason’s side in one sentence and turn to happiness. In the manuscript the first and last pairs are additions above the line. Auden’s objection to the word wager is that it makes faith sound like prudent calculation. Later in the paragraph Pascal’s word for the player who will not stake one life to win three is imprudent.
lenses.why: Three matched clauses set the stakes out on two sides, so the argument can settle reason’s side and move to happiness; Pascal added two pairs above the line. Auden says the word wager makes faith sound like prudent calculation.

grounds.claim: three headings on one pattern, four pairs, and the first and second member of each pair
parallelism builds two or more related words, phrases or clauses on one pattern
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae, rhetoric.byu.edu, parallelism

lenses.label: Scales
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: Pascal’s verb is to weigh: weigh the gain and the loss. Two sentences on, two halves of six words differ only in gain and lose, all and nothing. Setting opposites in matching phrases is antithesis. It makes the case for one bet, that God is: everything to gain, nothing to lose. In the manuscript a struck-out start went straight to the case of losing, and the words for weighing and If you gain, you were added above the line. Auden objected in 1939 that to let another world sway life in this one is in effect to suppose two Gods, and the prudent man will bet on the second.
lenses.why: Two matched halves put everything to gain against nothing to lose on the bet that God is; the manuscript’s first start went straight to losing, and the weighing was added. Auden objects that such reckoning in effect supposes two Gods.

grounds.claim: gain and loss named, then two halves of six words each that differ only in gain and lose, all and nothing
antithesis puts opposed words or ideas next to each other, commonly in matching constructions
grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae, rhetoric.byu.edu, antithesis

lenses.label: Game

notes.note: The French is *embarqué*: Littré explains the figure by the man who, once at sea, can no longer leave the ship.
notes.source: Littré under embarquer, sense 2 (Fig. Mettre quelqu’un dans une affaire, par une métaphore prise de l’homme qui, une fois en mer, ne peut plus quitter le navire)

notes.note: *Engager* is first to put in pawn; Littré quotes this sentence under the pledging of one’s word.
notes.source: Littré under engager, senses 1 (Mettre en gage) and 3 (Engager sa foi, sa parole), which quotes this sentence

notes.note: Pascal wrote *en prenant croix*: *croix* was the side of a coin once stamped with a cross, which Trotter gives as *heads*, and Littré quotes this sentence there.
notes.source: Littré under croix, sense 11 (Le côté d’une pièce de monnaie opposé à la face et marqué autrefois d’une croix. Croix ou pile), which quotes this sentence; Littré under pile [3], sense 2, gives jouer à pile ou face as the same game as croix ou pile; Trotter has heads or tails for croix ou pile at pascal/s03, block 142, words 153 to 155, and chooses heads for prend croix at block 143, words 37 to 38; all read 2026-10-03

notes.source: Brunschvicg’s text of fragment 233 (‘ces deux cas’); Littré under cas, sense 1

lenses.caption: The words belong to a voyage and a game. Embarked is embarqué, said of a man at sea who cannot leave the ship. Behind in wagering is en prenant croix, taking the side of the coin that Trotter has called heads. The reckoning goes by a rule the next fragment names, the doctrine of chance. In French it is the rule for dividing the stakes of an unfinished game, which Pascal set out in a treatise. The same fragment adds that people work for the uncertain at sea and in battle. Auden granted the word wager this much: it reminds people that elsewhere they act on faith, and willingly.
lenses.why: The words are a game’s, and the reckoning goes by a rule of games, the dividing of stakes, which the next fragment names; Auden grants the word wager this much, that elsewhere people act willingly on faith.

auden.says: In an essay on Kierkegaard, Auden says that however good the argument, faith is still a choice, and nobody can make it for someone else. He finds Pascal’s word and Kierkegaard’s both inadequate, and allows each some value. The wager reminds people that everywhere else in life they act on faith all the time, and willingly, so that religion cannot fairly be expected to differ.
auden.quote: Pascal’s ‘wager’ and Kierkegaard’s ‘leap’ are neither of them quite adequate descriptions, for the one suggests prudent calculation and the other perverse arbitrariness.
auden.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 8530-8541, on 2026-10-03; the page number 178 stands at the foot of the page. The scan drops most punctuation: the punctuation of the quotation is restored as in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 11, and the inner quotation marks are set as single ones.

auden.says: In 1939 his objection went further. Whether a supernatural world exists he leaves open. But to hold with Pascal that it ought to change how life is lived here is, he wrote, to split the chain of causes in two and in effect to set up two Gods, one ruling each world. The second God’s punishments never end, so prudence backs him against the first. Auden calls this the sin against the Holy Ghost, the denial that truth is one.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 46–47
auden.checked: read by the poet in search-inside snippets of the Internet Archive scan prolificdevourer00aude, and read again on 2026-10-03; the foot line for p. 46 (the number and the author’s name) stands just before the closing words about the prudent man. Read again by the examiner the same day, chained forward from the sentence on whether there is a supernatural world to the sentence on the sin against the Holy Ghost: the passage begins on p. 46 (after the foot line for p. 45) and its last sentence and a half are on p. 47

auden.says: Among his notes on existentialism Auden grants that accounts of choice such as Pascal’s wager and Kierkegaard’s leap have their interest as drama, and asks if they hold true. Of the few decisive choices in his own life he says that he had little idea, when he made them, of how much hung on them. He is thankful for it: had he known the danger, he would not have taken the step.
auden.source: “Hic et Ille,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 103
auden.checked: read in the scan of The Dyer’s Hand, research/auden/dh.txt, lines 4868-4904, on 2026-10-03; the running head ‘Hic et Ille [ 103’ stands above the paragraph

auden.says: In the Michigan class of 1941 Auden used Pascal to describe the two chief characters of *Othello*. According to a student’s notes, he said that Othello is exactly one of Pascal’s types, a man who meets life’s problems with nothing but feeling and a handful of moral rules. Iago has the mind Pascal calls geometrical: he settles everything by reason, and reasons faultlessly, though he neither sees the principles nor cares about them. The *Pensées* as printed here open with this contrast, of the mathematical mind with the intuitive.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 141 and 143
auden.checked: read in research/A_pearce_gap2.txt (Pearce pp. 137-146) on 2026-10-03; the page number stands at the foot of each page, before the next page’s heading. The scan gives a French name for the type Othello is said to be; as the OCR has it, the phrase is not one of Pascal’s, so it is not repeated. Fragment 1 is pascal/s01, blocks 0 to 8.

auden.says: In *New Year Letter*, the long poem Auden published in 1941, a few months before the course, the Devil purrs agreement when people contradict one of his lies too emphatically. He wonders aloud if the serpent in Eden was not, very nearly, the spirit of geometry, calls it foolish to look for salvation in logic, and asks when people will throw intelligence away and live by an order of the heart. Auden’s note to the first of these lines quotes Pascal in French: the mind has its order, by principle and demonstration, and the heart has another. Two more of his notes to the poem quote the *Pensées*.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (London: Faber, 1941), lines 483–527 and Auden’s note to line 497
auden.checked: read by the poet in search-inside snippets of the Internet Archive scans newyearletter0000aude and doubleman0000aude, and read again on 2026-10-03. Page numbers 33 and 34 stand at the foot of the two pages of the speech (33 with the signature c); they are not cited. The finisher read the sentence the examiner places at line 483 again on 2026-10-03, in full-text search snippets of this scan, of doubleman0000aude and of the public scan text of The Collected Poetry (1945): it opens with So when; in it people contradict one of his lies with too much emphasis, and he does not deny it but purrs. The Faber scan misreads the word for lie; the other two have it. The first sentence of the entry now says who is contradicted and how.

auden.says: Reviewing Kierkegaard’s journals, Auden puts Pascal with Nietzsche, Simone Weil and Kierkegaard among the writers who are hard to judge fairly. A first reading overwhelms: no one has spoken in such a voice or seen so sharply. On rereading, doubts set in. Each of them presses one side of the truth so hard that the rest is lost, and the reader’s first enthusiasm can turn into a dislike just as excessive. The more one reads such writers, he adds, the plainer it is that their life of feeling is badly out of order.
auden.source: “A Knight of Doleful Countenance,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 182–83
auden.checked: read in the scan, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 8724-8740, on 2026-10-03; the sentence begins at the foot of the essay’s first page and runs on under the first running head. auden.says: Edward Mendelson, in his preface to *The Prolific and the Devourer*, writes that Pascal was one of its models: Auden was reading him by June 1939, had written a poem on him by August, and that month called the book his *pensées*. Its second part opens by saying that, like Pascal, Auden starts from an observation and an assumption: that people are unhappy more often than happy, and that this is unnatural. He adds that Pascal overstated the unhappiness. The poem of that summer is “Pascal.”
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), p. 29, and Edward Mendelson’s preface to it, p. viii; “Pascal,” in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (New York: Random House, 1945), pp. 86–89

auden.says: In an essay of 1956 Auden wrote that among the writers on theology he knew at school and university, only Pascal was readable and shook his self-satisfaction. Looking back, he found something fake in the writing, a romantic taste for unhappiness that may have been what drew him; but Pascal at least did not sound like a clergyman, and would not let him put God out of mind when he wanted to. In talk that Alan Ansen wrote down in February 1947, Auden names the greatest aphorists, Pascal first, counts him among the untypical French writers he likes, and says he has no liking for Montaigne.
auden.source: Essay in *Modern Canterbury Pilgrims*, edited by the Dean of New York (James A. Pike) (London: A. R. Mowbray, 1956), pp. 36–37; Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden* (London: Faber, 1991), p. 25

caveats: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, the book that gives this page its point of view, was read only in snippets of a scanned copy, and so were *New Year Letter*, the essay of 1956 and Ansen’s *Table Talk*. Wording and page numbers were not seen on a full page.
What Auden said in class in 1941 is known from notes that a student, Donald Pearce, wrote down after each lecture, and his talk of 1947 from notes kept by Alan Ansen. Neither is Auden’s own text.

The English is W. F. Trotter’s, and its sentence breaks and some of its words (*feel*, *then*, *atom*, *the world*, and three of the eighteen uses of *you*) are his. In fragment 278 the French verb *sentir* can be taken simply as to feel.

Pascal’s additions above the line and the order in which he filled one manuscript page are taken from an editor’s notes and a modern transcription, not the manuscript. The order is the modern editors’ judgment, and they count the two fragments as separate notes, not part of the wager.

The printed order and the numbers of the fragments are an editor’s. Fragments 347 and 348 stand on different pages of the manuscript, and modern editors think 277 was written after 278. The paragraph on dignity and thought is known only from early copies of Pascal’s papers.
open: The Prolific and the Devourer was not seen in a full copy. Everything given from it (the view, its quotation, the definition of dualism, the two Gods passage, the sentence about Montaigne, the opening of Part II, the preface) was pieced together from Internet Archive search snippets of an OCR scan, by the poet and again by the examiner. The page numbers are inferred from the foot lines that fall inside the snippets (vii, viii, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34, 45, 46, 47, 72 and 73 were seen; the one for 34 is misread by the OCR). The research notes (C_auden_on_works.md) give pp. 46-47 for the sentences on the dualists; the foot lines put them on p. 47, running on to p. 48, with the two Gods passage on pp. 46-47, and E_pd_pearce.md, section 1.1, independently finds that the number line is a foot line and that p. 47 ends at the same words. A lead with the book should confirm pages and punctuation.

Examiner, 2026-10-03: the gloss of ‘dualists’ in the view was the poet’s own, drawn from the two-worlds passage. Auden defines the word himself on p. 31 of The Prolific and the Devourer (a division of the whole in two, one part good and one evil; theological, metaphysical or political), and the view now gives that, with Pascal’s kind after it. Three more sentences of that book bear on Pascal and are not in the list: p. 34 (the hope of ascetic dualists like Pascal is as vain as the Romantics’), pp. 45-46 (Pascal and Rousseau both lacked faith and made growth impossible, the one by taking away the needed energy, the other the needed intelligence), and p. 73 (Romanticism traded the old dualism of natural and supernatural worlds for one of body and mind, heart and reason; reason alone lets us love those we have not seen). The last would serve a lead who wants more on heart and reason.

New Year Letter was read in snippets only. The examiner chained the verse from line 483 to line 528: the passage on the spirit of geometry and the order of the heart is the Devil’s speech (he purrs agreement at line 486 and the quotation closes at 527), and the entry now says so. Line numbers are fixed by the marginal numbers and by Auden’s notes headed Line 497 and Line 527. Page numbers 33 and 34 were seen at the foot of the verse pages and 102 and 106 near the notes; none is cited. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the sentence of line 483 was read again in three scans. People contradict one of his lies with too much emphasis, and he purrs agreement; the entry’s first sentence said only that he answers a contradiction, and now says this.

The examiner found in scans two things the poet had only from remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md: Auden’s essay in Modern Canterbury Pilgrims (London: Mowbray, 1956), pp. 36-37, and Ansen’s Table Talk (Faber, 1991), p. 25. Both were read in snippets, and the page of the first rests on running heads taken to stand at the top of the page. The essay speaks of his school and university years, not of 1939 as the old entry let a reader think. Finisher, 2026-10-03: read again in snippets. The judgment that there is something fake in Pascal’s writing opens with the word Today, so it is of the time of writing; the entry said By then, which could be taken for his student years, and now says Looking back, with the year of the essay in the sentence before. Mendelson’s Early Auden, Later Auden (pp. 390-92, 398-99) was not seen and is no longer cited: what it was cited for is now given from Mendelson’s preface to The Prolific and the Devourer, p. viii, and from the essay itself.

Auden’s poem “Pascal” was read by the examiner, and again by the finisher, in the public scan text of The Collected Poetry (1945; the scan is a sixth printing). It stands on pp. 86-89, not 86-88: five lines follow the foot number 88, and the contents put the next poem at p. 89. The research notes (C_auden_on_works.md, section 11 and appendix H23) still give pp. 86-88 for the poem; the lines they quote are on p. 88. The list used to give the poem in one sentence of its own images (a gift, an orphan, a night one autumn). The finisher took that sentence out: the poem does not say what its Gift is and does not name its night, so a reader could not tell what the images stand for, and to say that the Gift is his reason, which would agree with the view, is a reading that no source here makes. The list now only names the poem. The same scan has “Voltaire at Ferney”, where Pascal is Voltaire’s one great enemy; not used. The research notes also cite “A Preface to Kierkegaard” (1944), which puts Pascal in the line of Augustine, Newman and Barth; not checked and not used.

The first figure tab (Reasons) drew no stroke on the built page, because the usual pairing joins only equal numbers of parts. The examiner set its join to the first two parts, the plural and the first singular, which are the two the caption joins. On the tab Reed the usual mapping drew a second stroke, from the first word to the image where it returns, which on a phone cut across the first; the caption joins the first word to the image once and tells the return by the word added, so its join is set to the first two parts as well. The artist, who was at work on the piece at the same time, proposed both settings in art.md and photographed them (shots/proposed-heart-0-reasons and shots/proposed-reed-0-reed, at 1280 and 390). The piece has been built several times since, and both tabs have been looked at: the finisher’s pictures of 13:00 to 13:02 UTC on 2026-10-03 (shots/finisher) show the one stroke on Reasons, as the open tab of the whole-page slices, and the one arc on Reed, each at 1280 and 390.

Pearce’s notes are a student’s. The OCR of his p. 141 gives a French name for the type Othello is said to be that is not a phrase of Pascal’s as it stands (it joins the words for mind and heart); the entry paraphrases the English gloss that follows and does not repeat the French.

The manuscript (BnF, Recueil original) was not seen. Additions above the line are given from Brunschvicg’s notes and from the diplomatic transcriptions of pages 4 and 8 in the electronic edition of Descotes and Proust, which were viewed as images (page 8 twice). The order of writing on page 8 (278 before 277; 277 written upside down at the top for want of room) is those editors’ inference, and the caption says so. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the editors’ account was read again in the PDF; it gives an order of writing for all eight pieces of the page (sections 7 and 8 and the closing Nota), and the line over the drawing of the tab Page now says that the order shown is the one modern editors think they were written in. The same editors say that the texts on these pages other than the wager are isolated notes and not part of that discourse; since the examination the caption says so itself, where before it said the two fragments were written around the wager. The examiner enlarged both images: on page 8 the first writing of fragment 277 has only the plural noun, and on page 4 the struck start of the weighing sentence goes straight to the case of losing.

Brunschvicg’s edition was read on French Wikisource, whose scans are printings of 1921 (vols. XIII and XIV) and 1925 (vol. XII). No page numbers are given for it, only section and fragment. That its classification first appeared before 1904 was not checked and is not stated.

The hosted text does not name its translator, and neither does the Project Gutenberg file, whose title page is that of a Dutton paperback of 1958 with T. S. Eliot’s introduction. That the translation is Trotter’s rested on remake/research/D_texts.md and on site/data/texts/pascal/index.json; the examiner confirmed it in search snippets of a scanned Everyman’s Library printing (London: Dent, reprint of 1956, first published in that edition 1932), whose note says the translation, first published in the Temple Classics in 1904, is William Finlayson Trotter’s, from the text prepared by Léon Brunschvicg. The statement that its numbers match Brunschvicg’s up to 513 and run one behind afterward was checked at fragments 511 to 517, 541, 603 and 605 against the French, not fragment by fragment. Finisher, 2026-10-03: checked at the far end as well. The last two numbers of the hosted text, 922 and 923 (pascal/s14, blocks 184 to 188), are Brunschvicg’s 923 and 924 on French Wikisource (Section XIV, which goes on to further fragments that this translation does not have), so the numbers still run one behind at the end, and no second shift lies between. D_texts.md says instead that only the last fragment lacks a number; the comparison at 513 to 515 shows the series shifts there.

No French passage is set beside the English. No French Pascal is among the files that build/tools/original.mjs lists, and adding one (its fetch command) writes outside the folder a poet may write in. So the French words are named in the captions and glosses, each no longer than a short phrase, from Brunschvicg’s text. A lead who adds a French text could set fragments 277 and 278 beside Trotter’s English: sait against feel, sent against experiences, sensible against felt would then be seen and not only told.

The third passage has 126 words, over the 110 that POET.md asks and under the checker’s limit. It cannot end one sentence later, with the order to wager, because in the hosted text the last word of that sentence is joined to the next speaker’s first word (word 132).

The lead for this piece proposes the wager as a table of four outcomes. The passage weighs two cases of one bet, and the table printed in Brunschvicg’s notes (Louis Couturat’s) has two columns. No table is drawn. Couturat’s three tables for the three steps of the argument could carry a shape lens if one is wanted.

Leads not pursued: the silence of the infinite spaces (fragment 206) and Baudelaire’s abyss. Auden’s only remark found on the first is his report of Valéry’s view (Forewords and Afterwords, pp. 361-62), which is not his own judgment.

Fragments 347 and 348 are on different manuscript pages (63 and 165, by the page numbers Brunschvicg prints beside each fragment). The second passage sets them on one plate because 348 is headed with the image of 347 and the edition prints them together; the caveats say that the pairing and the order are an editor’s. The examiner read the electronic edition’s pages for both (2026-10-03): the first paragraph of 347 is its Transition 5, on the paper RO 63-6; the second paragraph is counted there as a separate fragment, Transition 6, whose original paper is lost and which is known from the two copies, as Brunschvicg’s note 22 says; 348 is its Grandeur 9, on RO 165-1.

Auden’s sentence in “The American Scene” (The Dyer’s Hand, p. 313) follows the hosted translation of fragment 1 almost word for word (pascal/s01, block 2, words 31 to 50 and 62 to 69). This is taken as a sign that he read Pascal in Trotter’s English; it agrees with remake/research/D_texts.md, which says the course sheet names the Everyman edition. No statement of his about which translation he used was found. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the entry of the list that reported this sentence was taken out, to bring the list to eight, and stands whole at the end of notes.md; nothing printed now cites p. 313.
